items.text: What is the authoritative peer-reviewed review on speed reading, and who wrote it?

Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman, "So Much to Read, So Little Time: How Do We Read, and Can Speed Reading Help?" Psychological Science in the Public Interest, volume 17, issue 1, pages 4 to 34, May 2016.
What is the core finding of the 2016 reading-speed review on speed versus accuracy?

There is a trade-off between speed and accuracy. Skilled readers already average about 200 to 400 words per minute, and it is unlikely readers can double or triple that speed and still understand the text as well.
What share of total reading time do eye movements actually account for, and why does that matter for speed-reading apps that remove them?

No more than 10 percent of total reading time. Apps that flash one word at a time to remove eye movements are attacking a small part of the problem; the other 90 percent is word recognition and meaning-building, which the app cannot speed up.
Why does removing the ability to reread text (as rapid word-by-word apps do) tend to hurt comprehension instead of help it?

Normal eye movements let a reader jump back and reread a confusing passage. Rapid serial word-by-word presentation removes that option, and losing it tends to reduce comprehension rather than improve it.
Does the peer-reviewed literature support claims of reading 1,000 or more words per minute with full comprehension?
No. The 2016 review calls such claims "probably too good to be true." No source opened for this domain supports extreme-speed claims paired with full comprehension.
People who demonstrate dramatic "speed reading" on a passage usually turn out to be what, according to the review?

Skilled skimmers who already know the topic well. Without that prior knowledge, the same people remember little and fail basic comprehension checks, so the real skill on display is prior knowledge plus skimming, not raw visual speed.
What is skimming, and when does the research say it is the right tool to use?

Skimming is scanning quickly for the most informative parts of a text rather than reading every word. It works fine when the goal is the gist of a document, not a complete, defensible understanding of every clause.
According to the review, what actually builds faster comprehension over time, if not a speed-reading technique?

Ordinary practice: reading broadly, building vocabulary, and gaining familiarity with how a given kind of text is structured. Faster real comprehension comes from language skill and topic familiarity, not a trick.
Roughly how much time pressure does a Logical Reasoning section put on a test-taker, per test-prep sources, and how should that figure be treated?

Test-prep companies (Kaplan, Blueprint) put it at roughly 35 minutes for about 25 questions, a little over a minute per question. This is a secondary, test-prep sourced figure, not an LSAC-published fact, so treat it as framing only.
What is "chunking," and what classic study demonstrated it?

Chunking is storing many recognizable patterns through repetition, so a cluster that looks like noise to a novice reads as one familiar unit to an expert. Chase and Simon's 1973 chess study showed masters reconstructing real game positions almost perfectly after a few seconds, but losing most of that advantage on random, impossible arrangements.
DERIVED: Where does a well-drilled LSAT test-taker's real speed come from, if not from reading faster?

This is a reasoned inference, not a direct research finding about the LSAT. The best-supported explanation is chunking: a practiced test-taker recognizes an argument's shape (a necessary-condition flaw, a correlation dressed as causation) almost instantly because they have seen that exact pattern many times, the same way an experienced estimator reads a ceiling stain fast because the pattern matches hundreds of prior jobs.

You need to find out fast whether a 40-page homeowners policy even mentions water backup coverage. Is skimming the right tool here, and is it enough to decide whether to fight a denial on that clause?

Skimming is the right tool to locate the clause fast. It is not enough to decide whether to fight a denial. That requires a careful, full read of the exact exclusion wording, the definitions section, and any endorsement touching it, because a skim can miss an anti-concurrent-causation clause buried mid-paragraph.
An experienced restoration estimator glances at a water-stained ceiling and already has a rough scope in mind before measuring anything. Is that because he reads the ceiling faster than a novice?

No. It is pattern recognition built from repetition (chunking): the stain shape, ceiling type, and time-since-loss pattern match hundreds of prior jobs he has already scoped, so the answer is retrieved almost instantly rather than worked out fresh. This is the same mechanism proposed, as a derived inference, for why drilled LSAT test-takers get fast.
A friend tells you he can read 1,500 words per minute with full comprehension after a weekend course. What does the peer-reviewed research say about that claim?

It is almost certainly not what it sounds like. The 2016 review found claims like this probably too good to be true, and that people who look fast on a passage are usually skimmers with heavy prior knowledge of that specific topic, not people reading faster in general with full understanding.
Your study partner wants to pay for a speed-reading course to get through LSAT passages faster. What should you tell them, and why?

Skip it. The peer-reviewed review found no support for technique-driven speed gains with comprehension intact; real gains come from practice, vocabulary, and pattern familiarity. Drilling argument types until you recognize their shape instantly will do more than any speed-reading technique.
On test day, should you try to physically read every word of a dense stimulus faster, or focus on something else?

Focus on something else: recognizing the argument's structure quickly from drilled pattern recognition. The research does not support reading faster as a path to better comprehension; it supports the opposite, that pushing speed past a comfortable pace costs accuracy.
What is the classic citable source for anchoring, availability, and base-rate neglect, and what three heuristics does it name?

Tversky and Kahneman, "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases," Science, volume 185, number 4157, September 27, 1974, pages 1124 to 1131. It names representativeness, availability, and anchoring.
What is a heuristic, and why does the 1974 paper say heuristics matter even though they usually work?

A heuristic is a mental shortcut used to make a judgment under uncertainty without doing the full calculation. The paper's own framing: these shortcuts are "usually effective" but "lead to severe and systematic errors," which is exactly what the named biases below are each one example of.
What is anchoring?

A number a person is exposed to first, even an arbitrary or openly random one, pulls their later numerical estimate toward it. The 1974 paper's own term for this is insufficient adjustment away from the starting number.
Describe the wheel-of-fortune anchoring experiment, including the actual numbers.

Subjects watched a wheel of fortune, rigged to stop at 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Median estimate was 25 percent for the group shown 10, and 45 percent for the group shown 65. Paying subjects for accuracy did not reduce the effect.
A carrier opens a claims negotiation at $9,000 on a loss you have scoped and documented at $24,000. What is happening psychologically, and why does it matter even if you know their number is lowball?

The carrier's $9,000 figure is an anchor. Even knowing it is lowball, later "compromise" numbers, including ones you propose, tend to land closer to $9,000 than they would if no number had been stated yet, because adjustment away from a stated number is typically insufficient.
What is the procedural fix for anchoring in a claims negotiation, and why is it procedural rather than a matter of willpower?

Put your own documented number (a full Xactimate estimate) on the table first, before the carrier's number exists to anchor against. It is procedural because anchoring works even on people who know the number is arbitrary; the 1974 study found paying for accuracy did not remove the bias, so the fix is controlling who sets the first number, not trying harder to ignore it.
In a DFS salary-cap game, why can the listed salary for a player act as an anchor on how you value him, separate from his actual expected points?

The salary number is seen first and pulls your gut sense of his value toward it, the same mechanism as the wheel-of-fortune experiment. The fix is the same: build your own projection and value number before looking at salary, not after.
What is the availability heuristic?

Judging how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by its actual frequency. The 1974 paper's own illustration: seeing one car overturned by the road temporarily raises a person's subjective sense of how common accidents are, even though the true rate has not changed.
How did the 1974 paper demonstrate availability using a committee-size estimation task, and what were the numbers?

Subjects estimated how many distinct committees of different sizes could be formed from 10 people. Small committees are easier to imagine, so the median estimate for 2-member committees was 70, versus only 20 for 8-member committees, even though the correct answer is 45 for both (they are mathematically equal).

A dramatic house-fire total loss makes the local news. Afterward, a homeowner overestimates how common fire losses are relative to water-damage losses, which actually happen far more often. What bias is this, and why?

Availability heuristic. The vivid, easy-to-recall fire story inflates its felt frequency, while the much more common but less dramatic water-damage claims stay less available in memory, so the subjective ranking flips from the real one.
After one DFS lineup with a 150-to-1 longshot wins a major tournament, players start overestimating how often extreme-longshot stacks cash. What bias is this, and what has actually changed?

Availability heuristic. The win is vivid and recent, so it is easy to recall, which inflates its felt frequency. The real base rate of that build working has not changed; only its availability in memory has.

A trader sees one dramatic headline-driven price spike and starts treating that pattern as common, overweighting it against quieter day-to-day price history. What bias, and what is the honest comparison to make instead?
Availability heuristic. The honest comparison is the full, boring base rate of price moves over a representative stretch of time, not the one vivid outlier that happens to be easiest to recall.
Describe Wason's 1960 study and what it demonstrated about how people test their own hypotheses.

Subjects saw the triple 2-4-6, told it fit a hidden rule, and had to find the rule by proposing triples and getting yes-or-no answers. Most guessed "even numbers increasing by two" and only tested triples that fit their own guess, so they kept getting confirming "yes" answers, when the real rule was simply any ascending sequence.
What were Wason's exact subject results, and is it accurate to say Wason himself coined the term "confirmation bias"?

Of 29 subjects, 6 reached the correct rule without a prior wrong answer, 13 reached one wrong conclusion, 9 reached two or more, and 1 reached none. His study is the founding demonstration of the behavior, but the exact origin of the two-word label "confirmation bias" is disputed in secondary sources, so do not attribute the coinage to Wason by name.

An adjuster has privately decided a loss looks like wear-and-tear, then reviews the inspection photos looking mainly for evidence of gradual deterioration, discounting evidence of a sudden event. What is going on, and why isn't this an honest, neutral review?

Confirmation bias. The search for evidence itself is biased once a conclusion is picked first, the same pattern Wason's subjects showed when they only proposed triples that fit their own guessed rule, so the review is not neutral even if the adjuster believes it is.
What is the procedural counter-move to confirmation bias when forming a coverage theory or a trade thesis?

Write the theory down, then actively hunt for the single piece of evidence that would break it, before hunting for evidence that supports it. This mirrors what Wason's successful subjects did differently: they tested triples designed to disconfirm their guess, not just triples that fit it.

A trader who believes a stock is undervalued only tracks news stories and data points that support that view, and skips past data that contradicts it. What bias is this, and what single discipline would fix it?

Confirmation bias. The fix is deliberately seeking out the strongest available evidence against the thesis before adding to the position, the same discipline of hunting for disconfirmation rather than confirmation.
What is the sunk cost fallacy, in Arkes and Blumer's own words?

"A greater tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment in money, effort, or time has been made," even when that past investment has no bearing on whether continuing is actually the right call now. Arkes & Blumer, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 35, 1985.
Describe Arkes and Blumer's ski-trip experiment and its numbers, plus their stated reason people act this way.

Subjects were told they had already spent $100 on a Michigan ski trip ticket, then bought a better $50 ticket to Wisconsin for the same weekend and could only use one. Of their subjects, 33 said they would go to the worse, already-paid-for Michigan trip, and 28 chose the better, cheaper Wisconsin trip. Their own explanation: people act this way because they do not want to "appear wasteful."

A GC has already spent $6,000 in staff time and legal letters fighting a carrier over a $3,000 disputed line item, and keeps escalating mainly because of what has already been spent. What is this, and what should the decision actually be based on?

Sunk cost fallacy. The $6,000 already spent is gone either way and should not factor into the decision. The decision should be based only on the cost to finish the fight versus what is left to win, exactly as the already-spent $100 ski ticket should not have driven the trip choice.
What is a useful diagnostic question to ask yourself to check for sunk cost thinking before committing more money or time?

Would I start this today, knowing only what is ahead of me, with no regard for what I have already spent? If the answer is no, continuing is likely driven by sunk cost rather than by the actual remaining expected value.

A trader refuses to cut a losing position because he has already put so much money into it, even though nothing about the current setup still supports the trade. What bias, and what should the decision be based on instead?
Sunk cost fallacy. The decision should be based only on the position's current expected value going forward, not on how much has already been lost getting there.
What is base-rate neglect?
Ignoring the actual background frequency of something (the base rate) in favor of how well a specific case matches a stereotype or vivid description, even when the base rate was explicitly stated.
Describe the 1974 paper's "Dick" demonstration of base-rate neglect.

Subjects were told a personality pool was 70 percent engineers and 30 percent lawyers, or the reverse, then read an uninformative description of "Dick" that matched neither stereotype. Both groups rated Dick's odds of being an engineer at 50/50, ignoring the base rate they had just been given, because the description felt irrelevant to similarity judgment rather than prompting a fallback to the stated base rate.

A public adjuster hears one dramatic story about a carrier litigating a bad-faith denial and starts treating bad-faith litigation as a common outcome of any denial, when the real base rate of claims that ever reach litigated bad faith is low. What is this, and what question would correct it?

Base-rate neglect. The corrective question is: before reacting to this one vivid story, what is the actual base rate of denials that end up as litigated bad-faith cases versus the much larger number resolved as ordinary documentation disputes?
A running back posts a 40-point fantasy slate off an unusual game script. Treating that single vivid output as representative of what he normally does ignores what?
His actual season-long per-touch and target-share base rate, which is the far better predictor of next week's expected points than one vivid, unrepresentative outlier game.
What single question is the standard fix for base-rate neglect before evaluating a specific, vivid case?

What is the base rate for this category of event, before I let how much this specific case resembles a pattern change my estimate? Anchor on the base rate first, then adjust for genuinely new evidence, rather than starting from the vivid story.
What is the "illusion of validity," and what does it explain about overconfidence?

"The unwarranted confidence which is produced by a good fit between the predicted outcome and the input information." It explains why people feel most confident in a judgment when the input data paints a clean, consistent story, even though a clean story is no more reliable a predictor than a mixed one.
What flight-training example does the 1974 paper use to illustrate overconfidence and the regression effect?

Instructors noticed smooth landings were usually followed by worse ones, and rough landings by better ones, and wrongly concluded praise hurt performance and criticism helped. The real cause was regression toward the mean, not the feedback; the instructors were overconfident in a causal story that happened to fit the data they noticed.

An estimator feels very confident in a scope-and-price number because the visible damage pattern looks clean and consistent (a uniform water line, one obvious source). What should temper that confidence?

A tidy-looking pattern is not automatically a well-predicted one; confidence should track how often that pattern-match has actually held up once demolition revealed hidden moisture or a second cause, not how clean the story looks on the surface, which is the illusion of validity.
A bettor feels very confident in a model's pick because the model's story for why the team covers fits together neatly. What should that confidence actually be checked against?

The model's real track record of being right on similar picks, not how neatly the current story fits together. A neat-fitting narrative is the illusion of validity, not evidence the model is reliable.
What is the general fix for overconfidence driven by the illusion of validity?

Check calibration: ask how often judgments that felt this confident have actually turned out right in the past, instead of trusting the feeling of confidence itself, since that feeling tracks how clean the story looks, not real predictive accuracy.
What is the difference between a heuristic and a bias, using anchoring as the example?

A heuristic is the shortcut process itself (starting from an available number and adjusting). The bias is the systematic error that process produces (insufficient adjustment, so estimates cluster too close to the starting number). The heuristic is the mechanism; the bias is its measurable, predictable failure.
A course vendor claims "our speed-reading method raises your LSAT score by 12 points." What is wrong with this claim, and what two things should you ask for?

No source opened for this track supports a speed-reading-to-score-gain claim at all, and this track never states a point-gain number for the actual LSAT, per the zero-fabrication rule against score-gain claims. Ask for the underlying study, its sample, and its method before accepting any such number; absent that, the claim is unverified marketing.
TRAP: Someone cites Wason 1960 as "the study where Wason coined the term confirmation bias." What is the precise, defensible way to describe that study instead?

Say Wason's 1960 study is the founding experimental demonstration of the confirming-evidence-seeking behavior now commonly called confirmation bias, without claiming he personally coined the two-word term, since that attribution is disputed in secondary sources and was not resolved this run.
